subtopic_detail: A three day history of a painful swelling at the vaginal opening in a woman who cannot sit down
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a 28 year old woman with three days of increasing pain and swelling at the opening of her vagina on the right side. She says it started as a small tender lump and has become so painful in the past day that she cannot sit down or walk comfortably, and she has not been able to sleep.

She has had no vaginal discharge, no urinary symptoms and no fevers or sweats, and her last cervical screening test two years ago was negative for human papillomavirus. On examination there is a tense fluctuant tender swelling about 4 cm across at the posterior part of the right vaginal opening, displacing the opening across the midline. The overlying skin is stretched and shiny but is not erythematous beyond the swelling itself and there is no induration extending into the surrounding tissue. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy and her temperature is 36.9 degrees C.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant tender 4 cm swelling at the posterior right introitus displacing the introitus across the midline, no surrounding cellulitis or induration, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 12 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and review her again in one week
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not penetrate a walled off collection and are indicated only when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic illness, immunosuppression or pregnancy, none of which is present here. Treating with antibiotics alone leaves the collection under tension and the pain unrelieved (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Aspirate the swelling with a wide bore needle and send the fluid for culture
options.rationale: Simple aspiration gives immediate relief but the cavity reseals within days and recurrence rates approach 100 per cent, which is the specific problem that placing a drain solves. It differs from the preferred approach only in that it makes no attempt to create a lasting drainage tract (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess).

options.text: Advise warm baths and simple analgesia with review in 48 hours if no better
options.rationale: Conservative measures suit a small asymptomatic cyst or a very early inflammatory lump that has not yet formed a collection, whereas a tense fluctuant 4 cm abscess preventing sitting and sleeping needs drainage now. Waiting risks spontaneous rupture through the skin with a poorly healing sinus (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess).

options.text: Incise and drain the abscess and insert a Word catheter for four to six weeks
options.rationale: Incision through the vaginal mucosa just outside the hymenal ring with insertion of a balloon tipped catheter drains the collection immediately and keeps the tract open long enough for an epithelialised opening to form, dropping recurrence to roughly 10 to 20 per cent. It can be done under local anaesthetic in the emergency department without a theatre booking (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess).

options.text: Arrange excision of the gland on the next available gynaecology theatre list
options.rationale: Gland excision is reserved for repeated recurrence after simpler drainage procedures or for a suspicious solid mass, because it carries risks of bleeding from the vestibular bulb, scarring and dyspareunia. In a woman over 40 with a persistent mass, biopsy at the time of drainage would be the relevant addition rather than primary excision (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess).

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vaginal opening and drain through short ducts, so duct obstruction produces a cyst and secondary infection produces an abscess. The organisms are usually mixed vaginal and enteric flora rather than a sexually transmitted pathogen, though gonorrhoea and chlamydia should be considered and tested for where the history suggests risk. Definitive management is drainage with a procedure that keeps the tract open, either a balloon tipped catheter or marsupialisation, because simple incision or needle aspiration alone recurs in the great majority of cases. Antibiotics are added only for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression. In a woman over 40 a persistent solid or irregular mass in this location warrants biopsy, since adenocarcinoma of the gland is rare but presents this way.
key_points: Drainage is the treatment for a fluctuant abscess and antibiotics alone are not
Needle aspiration or plain incision alone recurs in the great majority of cases
A Word catheter is left for four to six weeks to allow the tract to epithelialise
Antibiotics are added for surrounding cellulitis, systemic illness or pregnancy
A persistent solid mass in a woman over 40 should be biopsied
explanation.pearls: Make the incision inside the hymenal ring on the vaginal mucosal surface rather than on the vulval skin, because an incision placed on the skin side creates a chronically discharging sinus that will not close.

subtopic_detail: Watery diarrhoea with a rising creatinine and a white cell count of 19 following a course of clindamycin
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 72 year old woman with six days of watery diarrhoea, opening her bowels around eight times a day with lower abdominal cramping. She finished a ten day course of clindamycin for a dental infection eleven days ago and has taken no other new medication.

She looks dry with reduced skin turgor and her abdomen is soft with generalised mild tenderness and no guarding or rigidity. Her white cell count is 19.2 x10^9/L, her creatinine has risen from a baseline of 68 micromol/L three months ago to 145 micromol/L, and her albumin is 26 g/L. Her temperature is 38.2 degrees C. A stool sample is positive for the organism by nucleic acid amplification with a positive toxin enzyme immunoassay. An abdominal radiograph shows no colonic dilatation and there is no free gas.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 145 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 68), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), lactate 1.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), stool nucleic acid amplification and toxin immunoassay both positive
data_table.Imaging: Supine abdominal radiograph with no colonic dilatation, normal haustral pattern, no free intraperitoneal gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start intravenous vancomycin 1 g twelve hourly for a ten day course
options.rationale: Vancomycin given intravenously is not excreted into the colonic lumen in meaningful concentrations, so it has no activity against a pathogen confined to the bowel lumen despite being the right drug. This route distinction is the commonest prescribing error in this infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start oral metronidazole 400 mg eight hourly for a ten day course
options.rationale: Metronidazole remains an option for mild disease but is inferior to oral vancomycin for severe disease, with lower cure rates and more recurrence, and this woman meets severity criteria on her white cell count and creatinine. It becomes the fallback only when oral vancomycin is unavailable (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start oral vancomycin 125 mg six hourly for a ten day course
options.rationale: A white cell count above 15 x10^9/L and a creatinine rise to more than 1.5 times baseline both define severe disease, for which enteral vancomycin delivered directly to the colonic lumen is first line in Australian practice. The low dose is deliberate because the drug is not absorbed and acts topically on the mucosa (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start loperamide with oral rehydration and repeat the toxin assay in 48 hours
options.rationale: Antimotility agents slow luminal clearance of toxin and have been associated with progression to toxic megacolon, so they are avoided in this infection. Repeat toxin testing is also uninformative because the assay stays positive for weeks and is never used to monitor response (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection

options.text: Refer for urgent subtotal colectomy and start intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for fulminant disease with megacolon, perforation, refractory shock or a rising lactate, and her radiograph shows no colonic dilatation with a lactate of 1.4 mmol/L. Fluid resuscitation itself is appropriate but is supportive rather than the definitive treatment (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection

explanation.summary: Clostridioides difficile infection is defined by diarrhoea plus a positive stool test, and testing should be performed only on unformed stool because colonisation without disease is common, particularly in hospital inpatients. Severity is graded on white cell count above 15 x10^9/L, a creatinine more than 1.5 times baseline, albumin below 30 g/L and evidence of colitis, and severity determines whether metronidazole is acceptable or enteral vancomycin is required. The precipitating antibiotic is stopped or narrowed wherever possible and proton pump inhibitors are reviewed. Fulminant disease with ileus, megacolon or shock requires oral or nasogastric vancomycin at a higher dose with intravenous metronidazole added and early surgical involvement. Recurrence occurs in about one in five patients after a first episode and is treated with a tapered vancomycin course, fidaxomicin or faecal microbiota transplantation.
key_points: Severity is graded on white cell count, creatinine, albumin and evidence of colitis
Intravenous vancomycin has no luminal activity and does not treat this infection
Enteral vancomycin 125 mg six hourly for ten days is first line for severe disease
Antimotility agents are avoided because of the risk of toxic megacolon
Repeat toxin testing does not assess response as the assay stays positive for weeks
explanation.pearls: Stop the precipitating antibiotic at the same time as starting treatment wherever the underlying infection allows, since continuing it roughly doubles the risk of recurrence after the ten day course finishes.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection

subtopic_detail: Jaundice persisting at four weeks in a thriving breastfed baby whose parents describe pale nappies and dark wee
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a four week old girl brought by her parents because she still looks yellow. She was born at term by normal vaginal birth, went home on day two and is exclusively breastfed.

Her mother says she feeds well, has plenty of wet nappies and has gained 780 g since birth. When you ask about her nappies the father says her poo has gone a pale creamy colour over the past week or two, like weak milky coffee, and that her wee sometimes leaves a dark yellow stain on the nappy. On examination she is alert and well perfused with obvious yellow discolouration of her skin and the whites of her eyes. Her liver edge is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and her spleen is not palpable. Her newborn screening test was normal and her mother's blood group is O positive with the baby also O positive and a negative direct antiglobulin test. Her total serum bilirubin is 148 micromol/L with a conjugated fraction of 62 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 per minute, blood pressure 74/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and well perfused, jaundiced skin and sclerae, liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, spleen not palpable, weight gain 780 g since birth
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 148 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 62 micromol/L (conjugated less than 20 or less than 20 per cent of total), haemoglobin 142 g/L (140-220), direct antiglobulin test negative, newborn screening normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer her today to a paediatric liver service for urgent investigation
options.rationale: A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L or above 20 per cent of the total is never physiological and never breast milk jaundice, and pale stools with dark urine indicate obstructed biliary flow that must be investigated before the surgical window closes. Outcomes after portoenterostomy fall sharply once the infant passes 60 days of age, so the referral is measured in days rather than weeks (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Reassure the parents this is breast milk jaundice and review her in two weeks
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is common at this age in a thriving baby but is an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normally pigmented stools, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after the conjugated fraction is confirmed normal. Pale stools and a conjugated bilirubin of 62 micromol/L exclude it outright (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Start phototherapy and repeat the total serum bilirubin in twelve hours time
options.rationale: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water soluble isomers and does nothing for a conjugated fraction, and in cholestasis it can additionally produce the bronze baby discolouration. Repeating the total alone also misses the fraction that carries the diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Check thyroid function and repeat the total bilirubin in one week from today
options.rationale: Congenital hypothyroidism and galactosaemia are part of the prolonged jaundice screen but both cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and her newborn screening was normal. A week of waiting on a time critical surgical diagnosis is the harm here (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Request an outpatient abdominal ultrasound at the next available appointment
options.rationale: Ultrasound forms part of the specialist workup and may show a small or absent gallbladder or the triangular cord sign, but a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis and a routine outpatient slot loses weeks. The investigations that matter are arranged by the receiving unit rather than sequentially in the community (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Prolonged neonatal jaundice).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Prolonged neonatal jaundice

explanation.summary: Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days in a term infant, or beyond twenty one days in a preterm infant, requires a split bilirubin as the first investigation, and the single question that determines urgency is whether the conjugated fraction is raised. Unconjugated prolonged jaundice is usually breast milk jaundice, hypothyroidism, ongoing haemolysis, urinary tract infection or Gilbert syndrome, and is investigated at a routine pace. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in this age group means biliary atresia until proven otherwise, along with choledochal cyst, neonatal hepatitis, alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency and metabolic disease. Biliary atresia occurs in roughly one in fifteen to twenty thousand births and its outcome depends almost entirely on the age at Kasai portoenterostomy, with native liver survival substantially better when surgery occurs before 60 days. Because affected babies feed well and gain weight normally, well appearance is the trap rather than reassurance.
key_points: Jaundice beyond fourteen days in a term baby requires a split bilirubin
A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L or 20 per cent of total is always pathological
Pale stools with dark urine indicate obstructed biliary flow
Affected infants typically thrive, so good weight gain is not reassuring
Outcomes after portoenterostomy deteriorate sharply after 60 days of age
explanation.pearls: Ask the parents to photograph a dirty nappy on their phone rather than describing the colour, because acholic stools are often reported as normal by parents who have never seen a pigmented stool and the photograph resolves the ambiguity in seconds.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Prolonged neonatal jaundice

subtopic_detail: Accumulated possessions blocking a woman's home after a fire safety inspection, without any rituals or intrusive thoughts
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic seeing a 58 year old woman referred by her general practitioner after a council fire safety inspection found that only a narrow path remained through her house. Her kitchen bench, bath and one bedroom are entirely filled with newspapers, plastic containers and bags of clothing, and she has been sleeping in a chair for two years.

She tells you calmly that each item might be useful one day and that throwing something away feels like losing part of herself, and she becomes visibly distressed when you ask what would happen if her daughter removed a bag. She denies any repetitive thoughts about contamination, harm or symmetry, and says she performs no checking, washing or counting routines. She acquires most items free from roadside collections rather than buying them. She has never had a period of elevated mood or reduced need for sleep. Her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 28 out of 30 and she manages her own banking and medications without difficulty.

data_table.Examination: Calm and cooperative with reactive affect, no perceptual disturbance, no delusional beliefs, insight that the accumulation is excessive but strong reluctance to discard
data_table.Investigations: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests, thyroid function and vitamin B12 all within normal limits
data_table.Social: Lives alone in her own home, manages banking and medications independently, adult daughter visits weekly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Arrange a professional house clear out with the council and family support
options.rationale: Forced clearance without the patient's engagement produces severe distress, reliably rapid re accumulation and loss of the therapeutic relationship, and it is reserved for immediate threats to life such as structural collapse or a fire risk requiring enforcement. The council inspection has not identified that level of danger here (Source: RANZCP: Hoarding disorder).

options.text: Start fluvoxamine at a high dose as the primary treatment for her symptoms
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are the mainstay for obsessive compulsive disorder but response rates in this condition are considerably lower, and she has none of the obsessions or compulsions that would identify that diagnosis. Medication is an adjunct here, most often for comorbid depression (Source: RANZCP: Hoarding disorder).

options.text: Start risperidone for the fixed beliefs about the value of her possessions
options.rationale: Her beliefs about the potential usefulness of objects are overvalued ideas held with retained insight that the accumulation is excessive, which is categorically different from a delusion held with conviction against evidence. Antipsychotics have no established role in this condition (Source: RANZCP: Hoarding disorder).

options.text: Apply to the guardianship tribunal for a financial and welfare order now
options.rationale: Substitute decision making requires impaired decision making capacity, and she scores 28 out of 30 on cognitive testing while independently managing her banking and medications. An unwise or risky choice made with capacity is not a basis for a guardianship application (Source: RANZCP: Hoarding disorder).

options.text: Refer her for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting discarding and acquiring
options.rationale: The specific adaptation of cognitive behavioural therapy for this disorder, combining motivational interviewing, graded sorting and discarding practice in the home, cognitive work on beliefs about possessions and reduction of acquiring, has the strongest evidence base and is first line. Engaging her in doing the sorting herself is what prevents the re accumulation that follows imposed clearance (Source: RANZCP: Hoarding disorder).

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder became a separate diagnosis in DSM-5 because it differs from obsessive compulsive disorder in phenomenology, course and treatment response, and only about a fifth of people with hoarding have obsessions or compulsions at all. The diagnosis requires persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, distress at the thought of discarding, resulting accumulation that congests living areas, and significant impairment or a risk to safety. Insight varies and is specified as good, poor or absent, but overvalued ideas about the usefulness or sentimental meaning of objects are not delusions. Excessive acquisition is present in most cases and is specified separately, and it is a key treatment target because sorting achieves nothing while acquiring continues. Comorbid depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder are common and worth screening for, and the safety issues of fire risk, falls and squalor are managed alongside the psychological treatment rather than instead of it.
key_points: Hoarding disorder is a distinct DSM-5 diagnosis and most cases have no obsessions or compulsions
Beliefs about the value of possessions are overvalued ideas, not delusions
Cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for hoarding is first line treatment
Forced clearance without engagement leads to distress and rapid re accumulation
Capacity is assessed on decision making ability, not on whether the decision seems unwise
explanation.pearls: Ask whether items are acquired free or bought, because free acquisition through roadside collections and giveaways is the pattern in hoarding disorder while compulsive buying points instead toward a broader impulse control problem and changes the behavioural targets.

subtopic_detail: A single ulcerated area that has not healed on potent topical steroid while the surrounding vulval itch is well controlled
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 64 year old woman in clinic who has had biopsy proven lichen sclerosus for three years, treated with clobetasol propionate ointment used intermittently as directed.

She tells you the itch that used to wake her at night has settled completely everywhere except one spot on the right side, which has been sore rather than itchy for about ten weeks and stings when she passes urine. She has applied the ointment to that area every night for the last six weeks with no improvement. On examination there is the expected pale atrophic change with loss of the labia minora and early narrowing of the vaginal opening, and within it on the right labium majus there is a 12 mm ulcer with a firm rolled edge that bleeds lightly when touched. The base of the ulcer feels indurated between finger and thumb. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy and no vaginal discharge.

data_table.Examination: Pale atrophic vulval skin with loss of the labia minora and early introital narrowing, 12 mm ulcer on the right labium majus with a firm rolled edge and indurated base that bleeds on contact, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and inflammatory markers within normal limits, urine dipstick negative for nitrites and leucocytes
data_table.Medications: Clobetasol propionate 0.05 per cent ointment applied nightly to the affected area for six weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Increase the topical corticosteroid to twice daily and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Escalating potent topical steroid for an area that has already failed six weeks of daily treatment is the classic reason invasive disease is diagnosed late in this condition. A localised area behaving differently from surrounding well controlled skin is the signal to biopsy rather than to treat harder (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders).

options.text: Take an urgent biopsy of the ulcerated area and refer her to a specialist unit
options.rationale: An indurated non healing ulcer with a rolled edge arising within lichen sclerosus that has otherwise responded to treatment requires histology, because roughly 2 to 5 per cent of women with this condition develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma and it arises in exactly this way. Biopsy is taken from the edge of the ulcer including adjacent skin rather than from the necrotic centre (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders).

options.text: Start topical tacrolimus ointment for six weeks and reassess the ulcer then
options.rationale: Calcineurin inhibitors are a second line option for lichen sclerosus that has not responded to potent steroid, but they are avoided over an undiagnosed lesion because of the theoretical malignancy concern and they would delay histology by a further six weeks. Steroid failure in a single site means biopsy, not a different immunosuppressant (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders).

options.text: Swab the ulcer for herpes simplex and start oral valaciclovir empirically now
options.rationale: Herpetic ulceration is typically multiple, shallow and painful with a soft base and resolves or evolves within one to two weeks, whereas this is a solitary indurated lesion present for ten weeks. The induration and rolled edge are the features that separate the two (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe a topical antifungal cream and review her again in four weeks time
options.rationale: Candidal vulvitis produces erythema, fissuring and itch with discharge rather than a discrete indurated ulcer, and there is no discharge here. Another four weeks of empirical topical treatment repeats the delay already incurred (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory vulval dermatosis that causes itch, pale atrophic skin, fissuring and progressive architectural change with loss of the labia minora, burial of the clitoris and introital narrowing. Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line and, used properly, both relieves symptoms and reduces long term scarring, and there is evidence that adherent maintenance treatment lowers the risk of malignant transformation. That risk is the reason women need long term review: about 2 to 5 per cent develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma, typically arising in differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia rather than through a human papillomavirus pathway. Any area that ulcerates, thickens, becomes fixed or fails to respond to adequate treatment must be biopsied regardless of how well the rest of the vulva is doing. Pain replacing itch at a single site is a particularly useful change in symptom quality to ask about.
key_points: Lichen sclerosus carries a lifetime vulval squamous cell carcinoma risk of about 2 to 5 per cent
Any non healing, indurated or fixed area needs biopsy irrespective of treatment response elsewhere
Escalating topical steroid over an undiagnosed lesion is the usual cause of diagnostic delay
Biopsy is taken from the edge of the lesion with adjacent skin, not the necrotic centre
Vulval cancer in this setting arises through differentiated intraepithelial neoplasia rather than human papillomavirus
explanation.pearls: A change in symptom quality from itch to soreness or burning at one specific site is the single most useful history question in long standing lichen sclerosus, because it precedes the visible ulcer in many women who later prove to have invasive disease.
